name: Artemis III region: Peak Near Cabeus B
note: One of NASA’s nine Artemis III candidate landing regions (Oct 2024), about 400 km². On a ~6 km high massif between Cabeus and Drygalski craters, about 35 km southwest of Cabeus B crater. This point is the region’s centre; NASA picks the actual sites inside it once launch dates are set, so click inside the outline on the map to test other spots. Outline: USGS (McClernan 2024) from LROC QuickMap.

name: Artemis III region: Mons Mouton Plateau

name: Shackleton connecting ridge
note: High point on the ridge joining Shackleton and de Gerlache craters, an area that LOLA lighting studies rank among the best-lit at the pole. Its skyline uses NASA’s 20 m LOLA terrain: the Sun is above it about 66% of 2027, close to NASA Goddard’s own lighting map (68%). On a crest a few hundred metres still matter, so use the landing-area check.

name: Ridge high point near Shackleton (88.8°S)
note: An elevated massif about 30 km from Shackleton. It is well lit, but Earth is hidden for long stretches: the classic power-versus-communication trade-off. Crest values are sensitive to terrain resolution.

name: Shackleton crater floor
note: Permanently shadowed crater interior: classic cold trap. Useful contrast with its sunlit rim.

name: Best-lit cell #2 (1 km map, 2027)
note: One of the best-lit cells in this tool's 1 km map for 2027: on average 70% of the solar disk was above the terrain, and Earth's centre was above it 55% of the time. The window summary counts any part of the disk, so it reads higher.

name: Best-lit cell #3 (1 km map, 2027)
note: One of the best-lit cells in this tool's 1 km map for 2027: on average 65% of the solar disk was above the terrain, and Earth's centre was above it 50% of the time. The window summary counts any part of the disk, so it reads higher.

name: de Gerlache crater
note: Crater centre; its rim hosts one of NASA’s Artemis candidate landing regions.

name: Shoemaker crater
note: Large permanently shadowed crater (ice science target).

name: Haworth crater
note: Crater centre. One of NASA’s Artemis candidate landing regions lies on its rim.

name: Faustini crater
note: Permanently shadowed crater.

name: Nobile crater
note: Crater centre; two Nobile Rim regions are among NASA’s Artemis candidate landing regions, and VIPER targeted this area.

name: LCROSS impact (Cabeus)
note: 2009 impact that confirmed water ice in a shadowed crater.

name: IM-1 Odysseus (Malapert A)
note: Intuitive Machines, Feb 2024. First US soft landing since 1972; tipped over, which cut power and Earth link.

name: IM-2 Athena (Mons Mouton)
note: Intuitive Machines, Mar 2025, Mons Mouton plateau near the south pole. Position approximate.

name: Blue Ghost M1 (Mare Crisium)
note: Firefly Aerospace, Mar 2025. Ran a full lunar day of operations.

name: IM-3 target (Reiner Gamma)
note: Intuitive Machines target: lunar swirl / magnetic anomaly.

name: Chandrayaan-3 Vikram (India)
note: ISRO, Aug 2023: southernmost soft landing at the time ("Shiv Shakti point").

name: SLIM (Japan)
note: JAXA, Jan 2024. Landed nose-down: the solar array faced west and only produced power in the lunar afternoon, a real example of attitude affecting power.

name: Chang’e 4 (China, far side)
note: First far-side landing (2019). Earth is never visible here, so it needs the Queqiao relay satellite.

name: Chang’e 6 (China, far side)
note: Far-side sample return, 2024 (Apollo basin). Relay-dependent.

name: Luna 25 target (Russia)
note: Planned landing near Boguslawsky crater; the spacecraft crashed in 2023.

name: Luna 9 (USSR)
note: First soft landing on the Moon, 1966.
